description: Hello, we love space and everything physics. We are building a website that tells the story of the “Abandoned but not Forgotten." We want to share the story of the rovers, landers, and probes NASA left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space, for school-age space fans. We want to make it memorable as well as a quick reference for anyone.
summary:
Our challenge was to tell the story of NASA's abandoned machines, which helped make today’s missions possible but are rarely talked about. Instead of stating the facts and events ourselves, we wanted the lost machines to tell their own stories. To do this, we created an interactive website where users click on a world (a planet, moon, asteroid, and more) and receive a postcard from a rover, lander, or other machine that rests there. The postcards mark moments like their first landing, a midway checkpoint, or the day of last contact. Each postcard contains a message, their location, the date, and their names. In the messages, the machines share what they found, what they achieved, and where they are resting now. They also link to relevant NASA pages to learn more about that fact. 

This project is meant to inform teen students and anyone curious about these machines about their significance. The personification in the postcards makes learning memorable and shows why each machine mattered. The progress panel at the bottom lets users track which machines they have heard from and reread their postcards.
details:
Our project is an interactive website where users click on a 3D world (the Moon, Mars, Ceres, or Eros) and receive a postcard from a machine NASA left there. Each postcard shows a location, planet of residence, date, and the machine’s name, plus a short message from the machine. Earth is in the foreground as the addressee of these messages.

The site is a single HTML page built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The 3D worlds are NASA 3D models displayed with Google’s model-viewer. All postcard text lives in a spreadsheet saved as a CSV file in our GitHub repository. When a world is clicked, the page reads the file and uses a card ID (world, machine, card number) to pick a random card from that world’s stack, without repeating until every card has been shown. The randomness creates a sense of discovery. The ID also links each postcard to its machine’s drawing, so adding a machine only takes a new spreadsheet row and an image. A progress panel at the bottom tracks which machines a user has heard from, using the browser’s local storage.

The postcards turn facts and events into short stories that are quick to read, memorable, and based on real places and dates from NASA. We hope this makes students curious about machines that helped make today’s missions possible but are rarely talked about.

For accessibility, the site has alt text on images, a phone layout, and text that shrinks to fit each postcard. We also put everything in a spreadsheet so other people can add machines without touching the code. The postcards are imagined voices built on real facts, and the site says so. All dates and locations come from NASA sources.

Tools. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, model-viewer, GitHub and GitHub Pages, jsDelivr, Google Fonts, NASA 3D Resources, NASA mission pages, and NSSDCA for facts, canvas for the postcard, and hand-drawn sketches. No special hardware is needed. It runs in any modern browser, even on phones. SI tools were used to help write and debug the code and for drafting and research.
